one_liner: Research C code for a ~3.8%-overhead rank/select bit vector that interleaves rank counters with data and predicts select positions.
what_it_does: SPIDER answers rank and select over a static uncompressed bit vector using about 3.8% extra space (the SEA 2024 paper's figure; snippet only). The repo is not a library: spider.c, spider-1L-select.c, ni-spider.c and ni-spider-2L-select.c are standalone programs that read a bit file from disk into global arrays and then run a timed loop of random rank or select queries (r/s) or an interactive query prompt (qr/qs). To use it you would lift rank(), select_hl() and the builders in helper.h into your own code.
how_it_is_fast: Each 512-bit cache line stores 496 data bits plus a 16-bit rank counter relative to a 64-bit top-level count kept every 63,488 bits, so a rank query costs one cache-line access plus a small top-level array that usually stays in cache, then up to 8 popcounts. Select samples the position of every k-th one (16-bit low-level and 64-bit high-level sample arrays), linearly interpolates between samples to predict the target cache line, corrects with a short scan of the interleaved counters, and finishes inside the 64-bit word with PDEP + LZCNT. The ni-* variants keep the counters in a separate array for comparison.
when_to_use: Reference design when you are writing your own rank/select for very large bit vectors (the paper reports the gain at 8 billion bits or more, snippet only) and want low space overhead.
Studying or porting the interleaved-counter layout; QuadRank's BinaryBlock16Spider is a Rust reimplementation of the same block layout.
Prototyping select with prediction (linear interpolation from sampled positions) on x86-64 with BMI2.
when_not_to_use: Any production use: there is no LICENSE file, so the code cannot legally be copied, and it is not packaged as a library.

Programs that need more than one bit vector or thread-safe reentrant objects: all state lives in non-static globals declared in helper.h, so even including the header in two translation units collides.
Non-x86 targets: it includes x86intrin.h and uses _pdep_u64 and _lzcnt_u64 (BMI2/LZCNT), built with -march=native.

Small or cache-resident bit vectors, where the single-cache-miss layout gives little; or workloads needing the fastest rank at any space, where 25%-overhead Rank9 still led in plain loops in QuadRank's measurements.
When you need reproducible competitor numbers: the repo only times SPIDER itself, and a reproduction question in issue #1 is unanswered.

integration.min_toolchain: GCC with -march=native -mpopcnt -mlzcnt (Makefile uses gcc -O9); C standard not stated
integration.platforms: x86-64 with POPCNT, LZCNT and BMI2 (PDEP)
integration.thread_safety: Not thread-safe to build (global arrays); read-only queries after construction share the globals, and concurrent queries are not documented

gotchas: Bits are packed MSB-first: the builder shifts each input byte in from the low end of a 64-bit word, and the 16-bit counter occupies the top 16 bits of the first word of every cache line, so input layout differs from SDSL/sux LSB-first bit vectors.
The builder reads the file one byte at a time with fgetc and ignores a failed fopen beyond printing perror, so construction is slow and a bad path crashes.

speedtest.h times independent random queries in a loop with clock() (CPU time, not wall time) and generates indices from two 31-bit rand() calls, so the figure is loop throughput rather than dependent-query latency; issue #1 (Dec 2025, Ragnar Groot Koerkamp) asks why the paper's numbers sit between typical latency (~80 ns) and loop throughput, and is unanswered.
The 16-bit in-line counter limits each top-level block to 63,488 bits; this is fixed by #define, not configurable.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Only as a design reference: for a usable ~3.3%-overhead single-cache-miss rank, QuadRank/BiRank (MIT, Rust crate) implements the same layout and in its own benchmark streamed 2.63 ns vs 2.81 ns for its SPIDER-style block at 12 threads; for select, SPIDER's predictive scheme is the distinctive part, and splatlab rankselect (PTSelect) is the sibling to compare for in-word select.
verified_claims_summary: The SEA 2024 paper (seen only as search snippets; Dagstuhl and arXiv are blocked here) reports 3.82-3.83% space overhead, the fastest rank for bit vectors of 8 billion bits or more (22% better than pasta-flat) and select up to 41% faster than existing succinct structures while nearly matching the best 12.5%-space select; compiler, flags beyond the Makefile's gcc -O9 -march=native, and CPU are not visible. An independent Rust reimplementation in QuadRank's repo (i7-10750H at 3.0 GHz, n=2^35 bits) measured the SPIDER-style block at 29.39 ns/query in a single-thread loop vs 17.75 ns for sux-rs Rank9 and 33.99 ns for RankSmall<1,11> at similar 3% space (derived from page data).
status_note: Stale research artifact (10 commits, last 2024-05-28, 5 stars, no releases) with no license, so treat it as a reference to read, not code to vendor.
